title: Multiple Row Subquery
description: Choose IN, ANY, ALL, and EXISTS correctly, including duplicate values, empty collections, nulls, and safe exclusion queries.

questions.question_text: A subquery that can return several rows must be paired with which of these?
questions.explanation: Multi-row subqueries need set-aware operators; plain `=` cannot handle more than one returned row.

questions.question_text: What happens if you use `=` instead of `IN` against a subquery that returns 2 rows?
options: The database picks the first row
A runtime "more than one row" error
questions.explanation: A scalar position expects at most one row and one column; multiple rows cause a cardinality error in MySQL. A membership predicate such as IN is the appropriate shape when the requirement compares against a returned set.

questions.question_text: `WHERE department IN (SELECT name FROM departments WHERE budget > 150000)` — with Engineering (300000) and Sales (200000) qualifying, how many distinct department names does the subquery return?
questions.explanation: Only Engineering and Sales exceed a budget of 150000, so the subquery returns those two names.

questions.question_text: What happens if a multi-row subquery used with IN returns duplicate values?
options: Duplicates are irrelevant — IN is a membership test
Outer rows get counted twice per duplicate
questions.explanation: IN only checks whether a value appears in the set at all; repeated values in the subquery don't change the outcome.

questions.question_text: What happens if an IN-subquery returns zero rows?
options: The IN condition matches nothing — empty result, no error
NULL is returned for every row
questions.explanation: An empty set for IN just means nothing can match; this is a normal, error-free outcome.

questions.question_text: Which statement about NOT IN with a multi-row subquery is TRUE?
options: It always behaves identically to NOT EXISTS
If any subquery row is NULL, NOT IN can silently return zero rows overall
NOT IN never has NULL-related issues
NOT IN requires exactly one row
questions.explanation: If the inner set contains NULL, an outer value equal to a known inner value makes NOT IN FALSE; an outer value with no known match generally makes it UNKNOWN. Both fail a WHERE filter, so a nullable inner set can unexpectedly exclude nonmatches.

questions.question_text: `IN (subquery)` is logically equivalent to which comparison form?
questions.explanation: `IN` and `= ANY` both mean "equal to at least one row returned by the subquery."

questions.question_text: A multi-row subquery used with a plain comparison operator like `<` will:
options: Never error, always pick the smallest value
Risk a "more than one row" runtime error whenever it returns 2+ rows
Only work if ORDER BY is added
questions.explanation: Plain comparison operators require a single-row subquery; multiple rows trigger a runtime error.

questions.question_text: Which operator tests equality against any value from a one column subquery?
options: = followed by an unrestricted multirow subquery
questions.explanation: IN is a membership predicate accepting a collection.

questions.question_text: Scores are 40, 70, 90 and thresholds are 60, 80. Which scores satisfy > ANY?
questions.explanation: Each qualifying score exceeds at least the threshold 60.

questions.question_text: With thresholds 60 and 80, which score satisfies > ALL?
questions.explanation: 90 exceeds every threshold; 80 does not exceed itself.

questions.question_text: What does > ALL over an empty subquery evaluate to?
questions.explanation: No returned row contradicts the quantified comparison.

questions.question_text: What does IN over an empty subquery evaluate to?
questions.explanation: No membership match exists.

questions.question_text: What is the effect of repeated subquery values on IN membership?
options: They do not multiply outer rows
questions.explanation: Membership is a predicate rather than a detail join.

questions.question_text: Why can NOT IN with a nullable inner column filter out a nonmatching value?
options: A null comparison can leave the predicate unknown
questions.explanation: WHERE discards unknown as well as false.

questions.question_text: Which guard requires a threshold row to exist before applying > ALL?
questions.explanation: EXISTS makes the nonempty policy explicit.

questions.question_text: Thresholds contain 60 and NULL. How does 70 > ANY evaluate?
questions.explanation: The true comparison with 60 is sufficient for ANY.

questions.question_text: Thresholds contain 60 and NULL. How does 70 > ALL evaluate?
questions.explanation: There is no false comparison but one comparison is unknown.

questions.question_text: Why can replacing IN with a plain join change row counts?
options: Repeated inner matches multiply join output
A join rejects all null outer values with an error
questions.explanation: A predicate qualifies each outer occurrence without transferring match multiplicity.

questions.question_text: A scalar = subquery unexpectedly returns two rows. What should be done first?
options: Clarify whether membership or a single value is required
Use COUNT(*) regardless of the requirement
questions.explanation: The correct operation depends on the intended question.

coding_problems.title: Find exact threshold matches
coding_problems.task: Return id for applicants whose score occurs in thresholds, ordered by id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE applicants(id INT PRIMARY KEY,score INT); CREATE TABLE thresholds(score INT);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO applicants VALUES(1,40),(2,70); INSERT INTO thresholds VALUES(70),(70);
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT id FROM applicants WHERE score IN (SELECT score FROM thresholds) ORDER BY id;
hints: Choose a predicate that accepts more than one row.
coding_problems.explanation: The predicate compares each applicant with the entire threshold result without multiplying applicants.

coding_problems.title: Exceed every published threshold
coding_problems.task: Return id for applicants scoring strictly above every nonnull threshold; require at least one nonnull threshold. Order by id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE applicants(id INT PRIMARY KEY,score INT); CREATE TABLE thresholds(score INT);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO applicants VALUES(1,60),(2,80),(3,95); INSERT INTO thresholds VALUES(60),(80),(NULL);
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT id FROM applicants WHERE EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM thresholds WHERE score IS NOT NULL) AND score > ALL(SELECT score FROM thresholds WHERE score IS NOT NULL) ORDER BY id;
hints: Choose a predicate that accepts more than one row.
coding_problems.explanation: The predicate compares each applicant with the entire threshold result without multiplying applicants.

notes:
## Match against a result set

A multiple row subquery returns a collection of rows for another query to use. The outer query must use an operation whose meaning accepts that collection. IN asks whether a value belongs to a one column result. ANY asks whether a comparison succeeds for at least one returned value. ALL asks whether it succeeds for every returned value. EXISTS instead asks whether the subquery returns any row at all.

Imagine a campus scholarship service comparing applicants with scores recorded by a review panel. The panel might record several thresholds, including repeated values, or no values yet. Choosing an operator defines what eligibility means in all those cases. Replacing an operator merely because it avoids an error can silently change the scholarship policy. Begin by translating the requirement into membership, existence, at least one comparison, or every comparison.

## Build a concrete comparison fixture

Applicants have scores 40, 70, and 90. Review thresholds contain 60 and 80. A membership query returns no applicant because none of those scores equals a threshold. A greater than ANY comparison returns scores 70 and 90 because each exceeds at least 60. A greater than ALL comparison returns only 90 because it exceeds both thresholds. These are distinct questions over the same tables.

```sql
CREATE TABLE applicants(id INT PRIMARY KEY, score INT);
CREATE TABLE thresholds(score INT);
INSERT INTO applicants VALUES(1,40),(2,70),(3,90);
INSERT INTO thresholds VALUES(60),(80);
SELECT id FROM applicants
WHERE score > ALL (SELECT score FROM thresholds)
ORDER BY id;
```

The output contains identifier 3. A subquery used with these comparisons normally returns one column. Several columns form a row value comparison with different rules and syntax; do not accidentally select extra diagnostic columns in a scalar comparison. Run the inner SELECT independently while developing the query so its shape and possible nulls are visible.

## Membership and duplicates

IN is equivalent in meaning to equality with ANY for a one column subquery. If thresholds instead contain 70, 70, and 90, applicants 2 and 3 qualify once each. Repeating a value inside the subquery does not multiply outer rows. Each applicant is tested against a predicate rather than joined to every matching threshold occurrence.

That distinction matters when replacing a subquery with a join. A join against repeated threshold values returns multiple copies of applicant 2 unless the query deliberately restores the required grain. DISTINCT may be valid for a membership rewrite, but EXISTS often states the intention more directly. The outer table itself may contain repeated projected values; membership does not automatically deduplicate those outer rows.

Use a unique applicant identifier in examples so the result can be checked precisely. When a report asks for unique scores instead of applicant identities, SELECT DISTINCT score expresses a separate projection requirement. Keep the decision about which applicants qualify separate from the decision about how their attributes should be displayed.

## Empty collections have defined behavior

When thresholds is empty, IN and ANY are false: there is no value establishing membership or a successful comparison. ALL is true because there is no returned value contradicting the comparison. This is sometimes called vacuous truth. Consequently every applicant passes the greater than ALL predicate over an empty threshold table, including an applicant whose score is null.

An application might instead require at least one published threshold. Express that additional policy using EXISTS combined with ALL. Do not assume that the mathematical empty set behavior matches the operational requirement. A missing configuration row can otherwise make every applicant eligible, while a query that demands an existing configuration can correctly return no applicants until review is complete.

```sql
SELECT id FROM applicants
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM thresholds)
  AND score > ALL (SELECT score FROM thresholds)
ORDER BY id;
```

This second query returns no applicants for an empty threshold table. The EXISTS guard is a business rule rather than a performance trick. Test empty inputs deliberately because normal populated fixtures rarely reveal the difference between these two interpretations.

## Null values introduce unknown

A comparison with null normally evaluates to unknown. WHERE retains true results and discards both false and unknown results. If thresholds contains 60 and null, score 70 is greater than ANY because one successful comparison is enough. The same score is greater than ALL only with an unknown result, because the comparison with the null threshold is unresolved and no comparison is false.

For ALL, any false comparison makes the result false even when another comparison is unknown. For ANY, any true comparison makes the result true even when another is unknown. If neither decisive outcome exists, unknown can survive. These rules follow the meaning of the quantifiers; they are easier to reason about by evaluating each comparison than by memorizing isolated examples.

NOT IN is particularly easy to misuse. With thresholds 60 and null, a nonnull score of 70 has no equal match, but the null prevents the predicate from becoming true. Filtering nulls inside the subquery is appropriate only if the business rule says missing thresholds should be ignored. For absence of related records, a correlated NOT EXISTS often gives the intended behavior more clearly.

## Worked exercise: applicants above every peer threshold

Take applicant scores 60, 80, and 95 and thresholds 60 and 80. The strict greater than ALL query returns only the 95 point applicant. The 80 point applicant fails because equality is not greater than. Changing the operator to greater than or equal would include that applicant. Repeated thresholds do not change either answer.

Now add a null threshold and keep the strict rule. The 95 point applicant no longer passes WHERE because the comparison against the null is unknown. If null means unpublished and should be excluded, add WHERE score IS NOT NULL inside the subquery and separately decide what an entirely unpublished threshold set means. Filtering missing values can create an empty set, so the two policies interact.

## Worked exercise: safe exclusion by related identity

Suppose award_records contains applicant_id values 1 and null. The requirement is to list applicants without an award record linked to their identifier. A NOT IN query over that nullable column can return no rows unexpectedly. A correlated NOT EXISTS checks whether an actual equality match exists and returns applicants 2 and 3 for the original fixture.

```sql
SELECT a.id FROM applicants a
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM award_records r
                  WHERE r.applicant_id=a.id)
ORDER BY a.id;
```

The record with missing applicant identity is not linked to applicant 2 merely because its own identity is unknown. The equality correlation makes that interpretation explicit. If the policy treats unknown award ownership as a reason to halt processing, enforce that validation separately rather than relying on accidental three valued logic to hide all results.

## Why aggregate shortcuts need proof

For a nonempty collection of nonnull thresholds, exceeding MAX(score) describes the same successful applicants as exceeding every threshold. The empty case differs: MAX returns one row containing null, whereas an empty quantified subquery contains no rows. Null containing inputs can also differ because MAX ignores nulls while ALL considers each comparison. Similarly, a minimum shortcut for ANY must account for missing values. A rewrite is justified only after stating which input constraints make these cases impossible or adding explicit handling that preserves the required policy.

## Errors, optimization, and related topics

Using equals followed by a subquery that returns two rows in a scalar position raises a cardinality error; it does not choose an arbitrary row. Adding LIMIT without defining a meaningful ordering changes the question to one arbitrary candidate. Choose IN, a quantified comparison, EXISTS, or a deliberate aggregate according to the requirement. Aggregating thresholds with MIN or MAX also needs empty and null analysis before claiming equivalence.

The optimizer may transform eligible subqueries into semijoin or other execution strategies. SQL syntax alone does not prove that the inner query executes once per outer row, or that a join rewrite is faster. Compare plans with realistic data after establishing correctness. Continue with [Subquery in SELECT](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/subquery-in-select), [Join Cardinality](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/join-cardinality), and [INTERSECT](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/intersect) to compare scalar results, multiplicity, and set membership.
